content: This systematic review examines the use of antiretroviral therapy (ART) in pregnant women with HIV who are eligible for treatment. Mother-to-child transmission (MTCT) of HIV is the primary way children acquire the virus globally. MTCT can occur during pregnancy, labor and delivery, or breastfeeding. Strategies to reduce MTCT include maternal and infant ART, cesarean delivery before labor or membrane rupture, and avoiding breastfeeding entirely. When these interventions are combined, the risk of MTCT can be reduced to as low as 1-2%. ART not only benefits the health of HIV-positive mothers but also plays a critical role in reducing MTCT. This review was conducted as part of a series of systematic reviews to inform the revision of the 2006 World Health Organization (WHO) guidelines on antiretroviral drugs for pregnant women and the prevention of HIV in infants. The findings contributed to the WHO's 2009 rapid advice guidelines, which recommend lifelong ART for all adults with HIV and CD4 counts below 350 cells/mm³, including pregnant women. These guidelines emphasize the importance of early ART initiation for maternal health and aim to minimize side effects for both mothers and infants. The objective of this review was to evaluate the current evidence on treating HIV in pregnant women eligible for ART. It assessed the optimal timing for starting therapy based on laboratory parameters or gestational age, as well as which antiretroviral drugs to initiate in women not yet on ART and which to continue in those already receiving treatment. A comprehensive search of databases, conference abstracts, and expert consultations was conducted in June 2009. Randomized controlled trials and observational studies were included if they evaluated ART-eligible pregnant women and used clearly defined ART regimens. Two authors independently assessed the studies for relevance, extracted data, and evaluated the risk of bias. Relative risks (RR) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated for each outcome. The review found no randomized controlled trials or observational studies addressing the optimal timing for starting ART in pregnant women based on laboratory parameters or gestational age. Similarly, no studies systematically evaluated which ART regimens to continue in women already on treatment. Long-term outcomes, such as maternal mortality and virologic or clinical efficacy, were not assessed in randomized trials. Instead, surrogate outcomes like MTCT and infant HIV transmission or death were used to evaluate the efficacy of specific ART regimens. Three randomized controlled trials and six observational studies were included. Key findings include: 1. In a breastfeeding population, starting zidovudine (AZT), lamivudine (3TC), and lopinavir/ritonavir (LPV-r) at 28-36 weeks of gestation reduced infant HIV transmission or death at 12 months compared to a short-course regimen (RR 0.64, 95% CI: 0.44-0.92) (de Vincenzi, 2009). 2. In a mixed-feeding population, starting AZT, 3TC, and nevirapine (NVP) at 34 weeks reduced infant HIV transmission or death at 7 months compared to a short-course regimen (RR 0.39, 95% CI: 0.12-0.85) (Bae, 2008). 3. In the Mma Bana study, there was no significant difference in MTCT at 6 months between the AZT/3TC/LPV-r and AZT/3TC/abacavir (ABC) regimens (RR 0.17, 95% CI: 0.02-1.44) (Shapiro, 2009). Both regimens achieved 92-95% virologic suppression at delivery and during breastfeeding. 4. The Kesho Bora study showed a significant reduction in MTCT at 12 months among breastfeeding women who started AZT/3TC/LPV-r between 28 and 36 weeks compared to a short-course regimen (RR 0.58, 95% CI: 0.34-0.97) (de Vincenzi, 2009). 5. MTCT was significantly reduced when AZT/3TC/NVP was compared to a short-course regimen at 7 months in a feeding intervention study (RR 0.15, 95% CI: 0.04-0.62) (Bae, 2008) and at 12 months in a population encouraged to exclusively breastfeed or use replacement feeding (RR 0.14, 95% CI: 0.04-0.47) (Ekouevi, 2008). However, some adverse outcomes were noted: 1. The Mma Bana study reported an increased risk of prematurity among infants born to women receiving AZT/3TC/LPV-r compared to AZT/3TC/ABC (RR 1.52, 95% CI: 1.07-2.17) (Shapiro, 2009). 2. Ekouevi (2008) found higher rates of low birth weight in infants whose mothers started AZT/3TC/NVP at 24 weeks compared to those on a short-course regimen started at 32-36 weeks (RR 1.81, 95% CI: 1.09-3.0). 3. Tonwe-Gold (2007) reported an increase in severe maternal adverse events among women receiving AZT/3TC/NVP compared to a short-course regimen (RR 25.33, 95% CI: 1.49-340.51). In conclusion, ART is a safe and effective strategy for reducing MTCT, improving maternal virologic suppression, and decreasing infant mortality in ART-eligible pregnant women with HIV. Regimens such as AZT/3TC/NVP, AZT/3TC/LPV-r, and AZT/3TC/ABC have demonstrated efficacy in reducing MTCT. However, further research is needed to better understand the side effect profiles of specific regimens for both mothers and infants.
